lesson.title: Is this the real model?
lesson.subtitle: The AI supply chain, fingerprints and signatures

video.title: Is this the real model?
video.format_note: Animated explainer, 16:9, flat Darsi colours on paper-grey backgrounds, one recurring teacher character. Narration in the lesson language; captions as separate files, never burned in.
cast: Mr Joseph Mwangi — computer studies teacher, Kenya (main character)
Dr Farah Rahman — university lecturer in education, Bangladesh (cameo)
Narrator — the Darsi voice (warm, peer to peer)

chapters.label: A free app in the staff group

scenes.visual: Cards: Shared in a staff group; Three installs; Who made it?.
scenes.animation: Each item arrives as it is said.
scenes.narration: Last week a file went round our staff WhatsApp group: “AI marking app, free, no sign-up”. Three colleagues installed it. Nobody knew who made it, or what else it did.

scenes.visual: The title card: the course, the lesson title and subtitle, the Darsi mark.
scenes.animation: Mark pops in; the title slides up.
scenes.narration: Today: where AI models and apps come from, and how to check them before you trust them.

scenes.visual: Cards joined by arrows: Datasets; A model; Libraries and plug-ins; Your app.
scenes.animation: Each item arrives as it is said.
scenes.narration: Almost nobody builds AI from scratch. An app is built on a model, trained on datasets, run with code libraries and plug-ins, all made by others. That chain of makers is the supply chain, and any link can be faked or tampered with.

scenes.visual: A list: A fake copy, with a backdoor; A real file, changed on the way; A file that runs code when loaded.
scenes.animation: Each item arrives as it is said.
scenes.narration: What can go wrong? A fake copy of a popular model, with a backdoor inside. A real model, changed on the way to you. Or a model file in a format that runs code the moment you load it.

scenes.visual: One big value, SHA-256: 64 characters for any file; one byte changes half.
scenes.animation: Each item arrives as it is said.
scenes.narration: The first check is a fingerprint. A hash function called SHA-256 turns any file into sixty-four characters. Change a single byte, and about half of the fingerprint changes.

scenes.visual:
Code typed out on a card:
import hashlib, binascii
h = hashlib.sha256(data).digest()
print(binascii.hexlify(h).decode())
scenes.animation: The code types itself out; the highlighted line lights up.
scenes.narration: In Python, it takes three lines. Compute the fingerprint of the file you downloaded, and compare it with the one the maker published. Same: the bytes arrived unchanged. Different: delete it.

scenes.visual: The quick check: the question and its answer cards, with the speaker beside them.
scenes.animation: The speaker slides in; answer cards drop in.
scenes.narration: Quick check! The fingerprint of our download matches the one on the page we downloaded it from. Are we safe?

scenes.visual: Two columns. A fingerprint proves: The bytes didn't change. It can't prove: Who made them; An impostor's match.
scenes.animation: Each item arrives as it is said.
scenes.narration: Only if that page really belongs to the maker. A fingerprint proves the bytes didn't change on the way. It can't prove who made them: an impostor can publish a matching fingerprint for their own file.

scenes.visual: Cards joined by arrows: Signed with a private key; The file; Checked with the public key; Really from the maker.
scenes.animation: Each item arrives as it is said.
scenes.narration: That's what a signature adds. The maker signs the file with a private key, and anyone can check it with the maker's public key. A valid signature says: this really came from them.

scenes.visual: A list: Official sources only; Files that hold only numbers; A list: name, version, source; And the fingerprint.
scenes.animation: Each item arrives as it is said.
scenes.narration: Then build habits around it. Download only from the maker's official page or an official app store. Prefer model files that hold only numbers. And keep a list of every AI tool the school uses: name, version, source and fingerprint.

scenes.animation: Each item arrives as it is said.
scenes.on_screen_text: App lab: is this the real model?
scenes.narration: In the app, check a model file three ways: genuine, with one byte changed, and from an impostor. Watch which check catches which.

scenes.visual: The quick check: the question and its answer cards, with the speaker beside them.
scenes.animation: The speaker slides in; answer cards drop in.
scenes.narration: Your turn. That free marking app from the staff group: what do we do now?

scenes.visual: The summary: AI has a supply chain; Fingerprint: bytes unchanged; Signature: who made it; Keep a list of what you run. Takeaway: Check where it came from before you let it in.
scenes.animation: Points tick in as they are said; the takeaway slides up.
scenes.narration: Uninstall it, and use only tools from official sources on the school's list. Remember: AI comes through a supply chain. A fingerprint shows the bytes are unchanged, and a signature shows who made them. Keep a list of what you run.

scenes.visual: A list: Write a long number; Add up its digits; Change one digit in secret; The total gives it away.
scenes.animation: Each item arrives as it is said.
scenes.narration: Try it in class tomorrow: make a paper fingerprint. Pupils write a long number, add up its digits and keep the total. A partner changes one digit in secret, and the new total gives it away.

checkpoints.prompt: The fingerprint of your download matches the one on the page you downloaded it from. Are you safe?

options.text: Yes: a match means it's safe
Only if that page really belongs to the maker

checkpoints.feedback_correct: Right: a fake page can publish a fake file with its own matching fingerprint. Get both from the maker's real source.
checkpoints.feedback_wrong: Not quite: the fingerprint only proves the file matches what that page published. Is the page the maker's?

checkpoints.prompt: A free AI marking app from an unknown maker went round the staff WhatsApp group, and three colleagues installed it. What now?

options.text: Keep it if it marks well
Uninstall it, use tools from official sources, and add approved ones to the school's list
Ask the person who shared it whether it's safe

checkpoints.feedback_correct: Yes: nobody knows who made it or what it does with pupils' work. Official sources and a school list close that gap.
checkpoints.feedback_wrong: Not quite: working well doesn't show who made it or where pupils' work goes. Uninstall it and use official sources.
